I am sixty-two years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou County since I was a young girl. I never went to school, but I know this land by touch and memory. Here on the North China Plain, the only sensible way to feed a family from a small plot is the double-crop system: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I have six mu of land, and at my age that is just enough for me to manage with help from my family.

This October I will sow winter wheat. I will use the rotary tiller to prepare a fine seedbed, because wheat needs a soft bed to establish its roots before the frost. I will plant the improved variety Jimai 22 — it is what my neighbors plant, it stands up well to wind, and the seed dealer at the village cooperative always has it in stock. For fertilizer, I will spread a basal compound fertilizer at sowing and then top-dress with nitrogen in the spring when the wheat greens up. I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I usually spray pesticides four times through the season to keep aphids and rust away. I expect about one thousand jin of wheat per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will rush to plant summer maize. There is no time to plough; I will sow directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage, just like everyone else here. I will use Denghai 605 hybrid seed because it grows fast and yields heavy ears before the autumn chill. Maize needs less fuss than wheat: two irrigations are usually enough, and three rounds of pesticide will control the borers and weeds. I expect about eleven hundred jin of maize per mu.

This is the rhythm my mother taught me, and it still puts food on the table and a little money in my pocket.
